paragraphs.text: In the consulship of the most glorious emperors Honorius for the twelfth time and Theodosius for the eighth, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, at Caesarea in the greater church: Deuterius, metropolitan bishop of Caesarea, together with Alypius of Thagaste, Augustine of Hippo, Possidius of Calama, Rusticus of Cartenna, Palladius of Tigava and the other bishops, had gone out into the exedra, in the presence of the priests and deacons and the whole clergy and a very large congregation, and Emeritus, bishop of the party of Donatus, was also present. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: Dearest brothers, you who have been Catholics from the beginning, and all of you who have come to the Catholic Church from the error of the Donatists and have come to know the peace of this holy Catholic Church and have held to it with a true heart, and you who perhaps still doubt the truth of Catholic unity: listen to us, for we are anxious for you out of pure love. When our brother Emeritus, still bishop of the Donatists, came to this city the day before yesterday, word was suddenly brought to us that he was here. And because, with a love that God sees, we longed for his presence, we hurried at once to see him. We found him standing in the square. After we had greeted one another, we urged him to come with us to the church, since it would be hard and unseemly for him to stay in the square. He agreed without any refusal. At that point we thought he would no more refuse Catholic communion than he had refused to come of his own accord, or had hesitated in the least to come to the church. But while he lingered on in his heretical perversity, even though he was inside the Catholic church, I addressed you, my beloved, as you will be good enough to remember. I said many things, which you heard and which no doubt you still remember as far as you can: much about peace, much about charity, much about the unity of the holy Catholic Church, which God promised and has fulfilled. In that sermon I was both speaking to you and exhorting him, and, as far as the bowels of charity within me allowed, I was in labor in that sermon with all who stand in peril of their souls, longing to bring them to birth for the Lord. For the blessed apostle Paul also said this to certain people: "My little children, with whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you." But even after our sermon, when he still persisted in that obstinacy of his, we did not think we should despair even so; indeed, we think we should not despair of any human being as long as he lives in this body. For when I said the day before yesterday that I had not despaired, I did not say it so that I might dare to despair today.

But the matter has been brought to this point: since he has come, and, so far as we know, has come of his own accord, his coming should not be fruitless for this church. For either, as we much prefer and desire, we shall rejoice with you over his salvation too in Catholic peace; or, if he persists in that obstinacy, which we abhor and detest, you ought through his presence to learn better what the difference is between Catholic peace and heretical dissension. He is bishop of the party of Donatus, but he was ordained for the Donatists of this city; and in the name of Christ we have already received these Donatists in great part into the Catholic fold, so that we rejoice that almost all of them have been joined to Catholic communion. But even of those who have already entered communion, some (not all, indeed) seem, as I said a little while ago, to doubt the Catholic truth itself, while others do not even doubt, but, still set in their hearts in the party of Donatus, offer us only their bodily presence, men and women alike, inside in the flesh but outside in the spirit. Therefore we think it good to question their bishop. If he has anything he can still say on behalf of that party, if after the conference held at Carthage, known to all, he has anything still to say, let him say it without prejudice to the party of Donatus, provided it is something he thinks may benefit us, in whose city he believes he was ordained for your salvation in Christ. And we shall reply without prejudice to the Catholic side, since at present no role of defense has been laid upon him, provided our reply can, as we think and wish, benefit you, with you present and him present: so that, if he has been led astray, he may not lead others astray; but if it was we who were leading people astray, then, with him present, who outside perhaps boasts a great deal, we may be refuted, rebutted, convicted and taught. I have said this so that he will not refuse to speak on the ground that he can say, "My party has laid no role of defense upon me at present." For it is not as though he did not speak after that conference, or did not come to this city after that conference, or has ever left this province; nor do we believe that after that conference he never said a word to anyone on behalf of the party of Donatus. I know what was said about us (I am speaking to you who have come from that party); I know what was said to you: that we bought the judge's verdict. I know it was said to you that he was of our communion, and that for this reason he did not allow them to say everything they wanted, and that he crushed them with power rather than accepting with integrity what they were saying. All these things were spread about after the conference, whether by him or by men of his communion. What does it matter by whom you are disturbed, when we want you to be at rest in Catholic peace? If he were absent, I would say of him to you: "Whoever is troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he is." For these words I have quoted are those of the blessed Paul against absent men by whom simple people were being troubled. But now he is present: let him just be good enough to tell us why he has come.

Brother Emeritus, you are present. You took part in the conference with us. If you were defeated, why have you come? But if you do not think you were defeated, tell us why you consider yourself the victor. For you are truly defeated only if you were defeated by the truth. But if you seem to have been defeated by power while you won by truth, there is no power here by which you could seem to be defeated; let your fellow citizens hear why you presume yourself the victor. But if you know that the truth was victorious against you, why do you still reject unity? Emeritus, bishop of the party of Donatus, said: The records show whether I was defeated or won, whether I was defeated by truth or crushed by power. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: Why then have you come? Emeritus, bishop of the party of Donatus, said: To say what you are asking. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: I am asking why you have come. I would not be asking this if you had not come. Emeritus, bishop of the party of Donatus, said to the notary who was taking down the record: Write it down.

And when he fell silent, Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: If, then, you have fallen silent before the truth, there was no reason for your coming except that you wished to deceive these people. And when he remained silent for a long time, Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: You see, brothers, that he has long been silent. I urge you to pray that he come to his senses; I beg you not to follow a man who is perishing. Nevertheless, since he has mentioned the records of our conference, where he said it can be seen whether he was defeated by truth or crushed by power: there are indeed many places where they swelled the records with superfluous and delaying submissions, working with all their might for nothing but that nothing should be done; yet with the Lord presiding and pleading his own cause, things came to the point they did not want. The case was argued and decided. But if we wished to read you the whole record... Now, in your presence I bind my brother and fellow bishop Deuterius not to be slow from now on to do as is done at Carthage, at Thagaste, at Constantina, at Hippo, and in all conscientious churches: that every year, during the days of fasting, that is, the forty days before Easter, when you are fasting most and have more leisure to listen, this same record of the conference be read through entirely, in order, from beginning to end, every single year. Yet, as I had begun to say, since we cannot read you everything now, please first hear the letter which we gave to the judge before the conference, in which we promised both how we would wish to be received if we were defeated and how we would receive them if we were victorious, so that the victory might be seen to lie not in contention but in humility.

Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, read out the letter: To our honorable and most beloved son, the most illustrious and distinguished Marcellinus, tribune and notary, Aurelius, Silvanus and all the Catholic bishops. By this letter we make known that, as you were good enough to advise, we agree in every respect with the edict of Your Excellency, by which provision has been made for preserving the calm and quiet of our conference and for making the truth manifest and safeguarding it. Trusting in the truth, we also bind ourselves by this condition: if those with whom we are dealing can show us that, when according to God's promises the Christian peoples, growing everywhere, had already filled a great part of the world and were spreading out to fill the rest, the Church of Christ suddenly perished through the contagion of the sins of I know not what people whom they accuse, and remained only in the party of Donatus; if, as has been said, they can show this, we will seek no episcopal honors among them, but will follow their counsel for the sake of salvation alone, and we shall owe them gratitude for so great a benefit, for the truth made known to us. But if instead we are able to show that the Church of Christ, which already holds the most fertile expanses of many nations, not only of the African provinces but also of the provinces overseas, with an abundance of peoples, and which, as it is written, is bearing fruit and growing in the whole world, could not have perished through the sins of any people mingled with it; if, further, we show that the question concerning those very men whom they then wished to accuse rather than were able to convict has been settled (although the Church does not consist in them), and that Caecilian was judged innocent, and they themselves violent and slanderous, by that emperor to whose examination they themselves, as accusers, of their own accord submitted their charges; finally, if, whatever they may say about the sins of any people, we prove by human or divine documents either that their innocence was assailed with false charges or that the Church of Christ, to whose communion we hold fast, was in no way destroyed by their offenses; then let them hold its unity with us in such a way that they not only find the way of salvation but also do not lose the honor of the episcopate. For in them we do not detest the sacraments of divine truth, but the fabrications of human error; once these are removed, we shall embrace a brother's heart joined to us in Christian charity, which we now grieve to see separated by diabolical dissension. Each of us, with a partner in honor joined to him, will be able to take turns sitting in the higher place, just as a visiting bishop sits beside his colleague. This can be granted on both sides in alternate basilicas, each anticipating the other with mutual honor (for where the command of charity has enlarged hearts, the possession of peace does not become cramped), so that when one of them dies, thereafter single bishops succeed single bishops in the former manner. Nor will anything new be done; for from the very beginning of the separation Catholic charity has observed this toward those who, having condemned the error of wicked dissension, have tasted the sweetness of unity, even if late. Or if perhaps the Christian peoples are attached to having single bishops and cannot bear the unaccustomed sight of two sharing the office, let us both withdraw from the scene; and once the cause of schism has been condemned and the individual churches have been established in peaceful unity, let single bishops be appointed in the places where they are needed by the bishops in the individual churches who assent to the unity achieved.

And while he was reading, Bishop Augustine said: Let me tell you, beloved, and recall a most sweet and delightful thing which, with the Lord's help, we experienced. Before the conference itself, when some of us brothers were talking among ourselves about this matter, namely that for the peace of Christ bishops must either be bishops or must cease to be (and we must confess this), as we looked around at all our brothers and fellow bishops, not many readily came to mind who would be willing to undertake this and offer this humility as a sacrifice to the Lord. We were saying, as people do, "He can, he can't; he will agree to this, he won't put up with it," speaking rather from our own suspicions, since we could not see their hearts at all. But when it came to making this public, in the council of all of us, so well attended, of nearly three hundred bishops, it so pleased everyone, and everyone was so fired with zeal, that they were ready to lay down their episcopate for the unity of Christ, not to lose it but to entrust it more safely to God. Scarcely two were found there who were displeased: one an aged old man, who even dared to say so rather freely; the other showed his feelings by the silent look on his face. But after the brotherly rebuke of all overwhelmed that old man who had spoken so freely, when he changed his opinion, the other changed his expression too. Hear, then, in what terms the exhortation itself was made, for the sake of him who said: "Whoever humbles himself will be exalted."

He read further: For why should we hesitate to offer our Redeemer the sacrifice of this humility? Did he indeed come down from heaven into human members so that we might be his members, and are we afraid to come down from our chairs so that those very members of his may not be torn apart by cruel division? For our own sake, nothing is more sufficient than that we are faithful and obedient Christians; let us, then, always be this. But we are ordained bishops for the sake of the Christian peoples; so let us do with our episcopate whatever benefits the Christian peoples toward Christian peace. Bishop Augustine said: For our own sake we must be what you are. What must you be, whichever of you I am speaking to? A faithful, obedient Christian. This you are for your own sake, and this I am for mine. So what you are for your own sake and I for mine, we must always be; but what I am for your sake, let me be it if it benefits you, and let me not be it if it harms you. See what was said; pay attention. He read further: If we are useful servants, why do we begrudge our Lord his eternal gains for the sake of our temporal eminence? Episcopal dignity will be more fruitful for us if by being laid down it gathers Christ's flock rather than scattering it by being retained. And while he was reading, Bishop Augustine said: My brothers, if we think of the Lord, this place set on high is a vinedresser's watchtower, not a proud man's pinnacle. If, when I wish to keep my episcopate, I scatter Christ's flock, how can the flock's loss be the shepherd's honor? He read further: For with what face shall we hope in the world to come for the honor promised by Christ, if in this world our honor hinders Christian unity? We have taken care to write this to Your Excellency, and we ask that it be made known to all through [?], so that with the help of the Lord our God, at whose prompting we make these promises and with whose aid we trust that we can fulfill them, even before the conference, if possible, devout charity may either heal or tame the hearts of men, whether weak or hard; and so, with minds already at peace, we may not resist the most manifest truth, and may either precede the debate with concord or follow it with concord. For we must not despair that, if they remember that the peacemakers are blessed, since they shall be called sons of God, they will far more worthily and readily want the party of Donatus to be reconciled to the whole Christian world than the whole Christian world to be rebaptized by the party of Donatus; especially since, in the case of those coming from the sacrilegious and condemned schism of Maximian, whom they even tried to correct by hounding them with the orders of earthly authorities, they sought them out with such diligence that they did not dare to annul the baptism given by them, and received some of those condemned without any loss of rank, and judged others to have remained undefiled in the fellowship of that split. We do not begrudge them their concord with one another, but they ought to notice how devoutly the Catholic root seeks with such zeal the branch broken off from it, if that branch itself labored so hard to gather back a small fragment cut off from itself. And in another hand: We pray, son, that you may be well in the Lord.

When this had been read, Bishop Augustine said: Listen, you who do not know; listen, I beg you. Thanks be to God that I am speaking in his presence. This case of the Maximianists, which I now wish to set out for you, is where they wrecked the ship of all their slanders, as though it were laden with bad merchandise. Although we raised this case of the Maximianists so many times in our conference, they could say nothing against it; that is, against our objection, inserted so many times, repeated so many times, dashed against their faces so many times, they could make no reply at all, because they could find nothing to reply. So listen to it carefully. Look, he is here, he hears me. If I am lying, let him refute me, let him compel me to prove it. The records themselves are not here, but let the case rest on them. Let us put up with any delays so that we may get to the necessary documents, if I prove what I am saying. If, however, he has doubts about it, or, God forbid, pretends to have doubts, then, if he will allow me to say so, let him not enter communion if I do not prove it. But if he already knows that I am telling the truth, and knows that the reason they refused to answer was that they could find no answer, I ask you to judge for yourselves which is more tolerable: to receive in his rank a man condemned by themselves, or to acknowledge as a brother a man never convicted by them. Pay attention, I beg you; hear the story.

There was a certain Maximian, a deacon of Carthage in the party of Donatus. Whether through his own pride or, as they themselves think, through his own righteousness, he offended his bishop, that is, Primian of Carthage: unjustly, if he, being proud, offended a better man; or justly, if he, being upright, offended a less upright one. He was excommunicated by Primian. He went to the neighboring bishops, stirred up ill will against Primian, and accused him before them. They came to Carthage. The many Donatist bishops who came wanted Primian to appear before them, just as the forefathers of these men wanted Caecilian to appear before them. Recognizing the faction, Primian refused to appear before these men, just as Caecilian refused to appear before those. Primian was condemned in his absence by these men, just as Caecilian was condemned in his absence by those. What a picture of events God chose to set before our eyes in recent times, since oblivion was already blotting out what was too ancient! He was condemned in his absence. Primian was restored to communion by other bishops of the party of Donatus; or rather, since they had not deposed him, he was confirmed in his see. The Maximianists were condemned, just as Donatus deserved to be condemned by foreign bishops from overseas when Caecilian was acquitted. Maximian was condemned together with his twelve ordainers. The faction itself indeed included a great many; there were perhaps a hundred bishops. But so that a greater cutting-off might not occur, these men chose to depose a few rather than impose discipline on many. They condemned only those who had taken part in the ordination of Maximian when he was unlawfully raised up as bishop against his own bishop; the rest who were in that faction, if they wished to return to the church, were to be allowed to keep their ranks. By their own words, indeed, they showed that these people were outside the church; for anyone you urge to come in is outside. So a day was fixed, and if they returned by that day nothing said against Primian would count against them; they confirmed this by the decree of Bagai, and Maximian was condemned with the twelve. Then they set about having the condemned driven out of the basilicas. Judges were petitioned, proconsuls were petitioned, the episcopal council of Bagai was cited in court. The others were called heretics, they were shown to be condemned, orders were obtained, forces were gathered, and they went to eject from the basilicas men who had been condemned and persisted in their obstinacy. When these had been condemned, the congregations that supported them resisted; where they could not hold out, they were defeated, and in place of those who were defeated and expelled, others were ordained. Of these we know two, to say nothing of the rest: one, Felician of Musti, the other, Praetextatus of Assuras. After two or three years, through Optatus the Gildonian, after many persecutions had been inflicted on them through judicial proceedings and all the severity of the authorities, they received them back in their ranks. After their condemnation, after their expulsion, after the persecutions, they received them in their ranks and took them as associates and colleagues. For in place of one of them, Praetextatus of Assuras, they had already ordained another man named Rogatus, who is now a Catholic, and whose tongue and hand their army, that is, a band of circumcellions, cut off. And those who, during the very time when the condemned men were outside, nearly three years, were baptized by the condemned, were baptized outside the church of these people, and yet they were received just as they were. No one said, "You do not have baptism, because you were baptized outside." And yet anyone who comes from Ephesus, from Smyrna, from Thessalonica, from the other churches which the apostles planted by their labor, and to which, as we read, the apostles' letters were sent, letters we hear read aloud in church, is rebaptized.

The sentence is on record, and from what we have heard from our brother himself (may God make him our brother at peace), it was this very Emeritus who pronounced the sentence by which they were condemned. Let that sentence be read, the one by which they were condemned. Then let the sentence be read by which these men's forebears condemned Caecilian, and let us see who were made out to be the worse offenders, who were punished with the heavier sentence, who were condemned with the greater uproar. In it he said: "For although the hollow of a poisoned womb long concealed the harmful offspring of the viper's seed, and the moist clots of conceived wickedness slowly warmed themselves into the limbs of asps, yet once its covering vanished the venom conceived could no longer be hidden. For though late, the pregnant desires of wickedness have brought forth their parricide and their crime, now made public, as was foretold long ago: 'He travailed with injustice, conceived sorrow, and brought forth iniquity.' But since a clear sky now shines out of the cloud, and the thicket of crimes is no longer tangled, now that the names have been marked out for punishment (for before this there had been indulgence), while we still let the line of clemency run, the case has found those whom it must punish." And among other things: "Let us speak, dearest brothers, of the causes of the schism, since we can no longer keep silent about the persons. Maximian, rival of the faith, adulterer of the truth, enemy of mother Church, minister of Dathan, Korah and Abiram..." These are the words of Donatus' party against the Maximianists, delivered, as we have heard, at this man's dictation. Now you know who Dathan, Korah and Abiram were. They were the first to make a schism, and the usual punishment was not enough for them: the earth opened and swallowed them alive. "Maximian, minister of Dathan, Korah and Abiram" (these are his own words) "the thunderbolt of our sentence has hurled out of the bosom of peace." Listen further: "And the fact," he says, "that the gaping earth has not yet swallowed him up means it has kept him in the upper world for a greater judgment. For had he been snatched away, he would have profited by the short cut of his death; now he gathers the interest on a heavier debt, since he is a dead man living among the living." These are the words of the man condemning Maximian, or rather, as he himself puts it, thundering at him "with truth-speaking mouth." And yet they were received back, those asps, vipers, parricides, and the baptism given by the asp, the viper, the parricide is not exsufflated! You have heard how great a fire of eloquence blazed up when it found hay it could set alight. Brother Emeritus, you embraced your brother Felician, condemned by the thunderbolt of your own mouth; acknowledge too your brother Deuterius, who is joined to you even by kinship.

My brothers, whenever we raised this case of the Maximianists against them during the conference (I have set it out for you as well as I could), he kept more silent about it than he keeps silent about everything now. Let them not hide behind evasions, which are not a defense but a flight. For they say that they granted them a period of grace and received them back within that period. This is false. Twelve were condemned along with Maximian, while the rest had not been present at his ordination when hands were laid on him. It was to these that they granted the period of grace. For these are his own words: "Nor," he says, "is he alone condemned by the just death of his crime; the chain of sacrilege drags many others into partnership in the crime, of whom it is written: 'The venom of asps is under their lips; their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness. Their feet are swift to shed blood. Ruin and misery are in their ways, and the way of peace they have not known. There is no fear of God before their eyes.' We would indeed rather not cut away a joint of what is, as it were, our own body. But since the pestilent rot of a festering wound finds more relief in being cut out than in being left to medicines, a more wholesome course has been found: lest the deadly poison creep through all the limbs, the wound that has arisen is to be cut off at the cost of a brief pain." So he names twelve as guilty of the notorious crime, among them Felician and Praetextatus, though the names of all of them do not come to my mind. And then he goes on: "Know that those who by the deadly work of perdition defiled the filthy vessel with the dregs they gathered, and also those who were once clergy of the church of Carthage and who, by taking part in the crime, acted as go-betweens for an unlawful incest, have been condemned by the judgment of God presiding, through the truth-speaking mouth of the general council. But those whose plantings were not polluted by the shoots of the sacrilegious sapling, that is, those who out of a modest regard for the faith drew back their own hands from the head of Maximian, we have permitted to return to mother Church." They wanted to polish up their own image, since they were pardoning the sacrilegious and opening a way back to open schismatics. What is this, I ask? Let him only deign to explain to me how the shoots of the sacrilegious sapling did not pollute their plantings. Why do you grant them a period of grace if they could have had no part in Maximian's schism? But if they are partners in the faction, even though they were not present at the ordination, how is it that Maximian does not defile them, while Caecilian, condemned once in his absence and acquitted three times in his presence, defiles the whole world? An African does not defile Africans, a living man the living, a known man those who know him, a partner his associates; and yet Caecilian defiles those overseas, defiles those far away, defiles those who never knew him, defiles those not yet born? Felician, whom you condemned, sat with you, and did he not defile you? I never saw him; you knew him. I believe him innocent; you condemned him as guilty. Or if you admit that you received an innocent man, you admit that you condemned an innocent man.

And yet, my brothers, we do not begrudge them their concord. They have put an end to the diabolical hatreds stirred up among themselves and, as they suppose, have returned to peace. But this is what I say: if a broken branch sought out a smaller branch broken off from itself, with what care ought the tree itself to seek the branch broken off from it? That is why we sweat, that is why we toil, that is why we have faced danger amid their weapons and the bloody frenzy of the Circumcellions, and still endure what remains of them with whatever patience God has granted us: so that the tree may seek the branch, so that the flock of Christ's fold may seek the lost sheep. If we are endowed with a shepherd's heart, we must squeeze ourselves through hedges and thorns. Even with torn limbs, let us seek the sheep and carry it back with joy to the Shepherd and Prince of all. We have said a great deal, weary though we are, and yet our brother, on whose account we say these things to you, to whom we say them as well, and for whose sake we are doing so much, still stands obstinate. Cruel stubbornness thinks itself constancy. Let him no longer glory in a vain and false strength. Let him hear the apostle saying: "Strength is made perfect in weakness." Let us pray for him. How do we know what God wills? As it is written, "Many are the thoughts in a man's heart, but the counsel of the Lord stands for ever."
(P. 187, line 16, Knöll's edition). PROCEEDINGS WITH EMERITUS THE DONATIST, IN ONE BOOK.

Some time after the conference we held with the Donatist heretics, it became necessary for us to travel to Mauretania Caesariensis. There, in Caesarea itself, we saw Emeritus, the Donatist bishop. He was one of the seven they had chosen to defend their cause, and he had worked harder than anyone else in that cause. What we did with him, in the presence of the bishops of that province and the people of the church of Caesarea, is recorded in the ecclesiastical proceedings, which are kept among my minor works. Caesarea was the city where he was both a citizen and the bishop of the heretics I have mentioned. There, finding nothing to answer, he listened as if he were mute to my whole address, which I delivered about the Maximianists alone in his hearing and in the hearing of all who were present,

This book, or these proceedings, begins as follows: "In the consulship of the most glorious Honorius Augustus, for the twelfth time, and Constantius, for the second time, most distinguished men, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October, at Caesarea, in the principal church."
